en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Chapter on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Pairs 24.
The Training Rule on the Rain-Cloak.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Blessed One had authorized the rainy-season robe for the monks.
The group of six monks, thinking, “The Blessed One has authorized the rainy-season robe,” sought out a rainy-season robe-cloth even beforehand.
They put them on only after they have been worn out;
when their rainy-season robes are worn out, they let their naked bodies be rained upon.
Those monks who have few desires... [and so forth]... they criticize, grumble, and complain:

“How can the group-of-six monks seek out a rainy-season robe in advance, wear it after having made it in advance, and then, when their rainy-season robe is worn out, expose their naked bodies to the rain?
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One.
… [The Buddha said: “Is it true, monks, that you seek out a rainy-season robe in advance?”
“Having prepared it beforehand, why do you put it on now?
Being naked, you let the rain fall upon your body because your rainy-season robe has worn out?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:

“… How can you, foolish men, seek out a rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikacīvara*) in advance, and having made it in advance, wear it? When your rainy-season robe is worn out, you will stand naked under the rain.
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so forth].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“When one month of the hot season remains, a monk may seek a rain-cloak; when half a month of the hot season remains, having made it, he should wear it.

If he should seek a rain-cloak when less than one month of the hot season remains, or should wear it having made it when less than half a month of the hot season remains, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.”
“When one month of the hot season remains,” a monk may seek out a rain-season robe (*vassikasāṭikacīvara*).

He should approach those people who have previously given rain-season robes and say to them: “It is the time for a rain-season robe; it is the season for a rain-season robe; other people are also giving rain-season robes. He must not say:
“Give me a rain-season robe,” “Bring me a rain-season robe,” “Exchange [something] for a rain-season robe for me,” or “Purchase a rain-season robe for me.”
“Having determined that ‘half a month remains of the hot season,’ one should put it on.
Having determined this when half a month remains of the hot season, one should put it on.
“If less than a month remains of the hot season...”
If, when more than one month of the summer remains, he seeks a rain-cloak, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If, thinking "less than half a month of the summer remains," he makes use of it or wears it when more than half a month of the summer still remains, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.
It should be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.
And thus, monks, it should be relinquished:
…pe…

“Venerable sir, this rainy-season robe-cloth of mine was sought after when more than one month of the hot season remained, and it was made and worn when more than half a month of the hot season remained;
it is to be relinquished. I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.
…pe… “He should give it back” …pe…
"May he give... [and so on] ... "I give it to the Venerable One.

If, when more than one month of the hot season remains, one perceives that more than one month remains and seeks out a rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikacīvara*), it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).

If, when more than one month remains of the hot season, he searches for a rainy-season robe while being in doubt [about the time], it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).

If, when more than one month remains of the hot season, he searches for a rainy-season robe perceiving it to be less [than one month remaining], it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If, when more than half a month remains of the hot season, he makes the perception that more than [one month] remains and wears it, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.

If, when more than one and a half months of the hot season remain, he wears it while being in doubt [as to whether the time has passed], it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If, when more than one and a half months of the hot season remain, he wears it perceiving it to be less [than that time], it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If he lets his body be rained upon naked despite having a rainy-season robe (vassikasāṭikā), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If less than one month remains of the hot season, and he perceives it as more, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If less than one month remains of the hot season, and he is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If less than one month remains of the hot season, and he perceives it as less, there is no offense.
If less than half a month remains of the summer retreat, and one perceives it as more, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If less than half a month remains of the summer retreat, and one is uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If less than half a month remains of the summer retreat, and one perceives it as less, there is no offense.
There is no offense if he seeks a rain-cloak thinking, "One month of the hot season remains," or if,
having made it up, he wears it thinking, "Half a month of the hot season remains."
If one seeks a rainy-season robe thinking,
"Less than a month remains of the summer," or wears it after making it up thinking,
"Less than half a month remains of the summer," and the rains retreat is postponed once the rainy-season robe has been sought, [there is an offense].
If one has worn a rain-cloak, the rains-retreat is extended; it should be washed and stored away, and put on again at the proper time.
This applies to one whose robe has been torn or whose robe has been lost.
In times of distress,
for one who is insane,
and for the first offender.
The training rule on the rains-bathing cloth, the fourth, is concluded.
